title: “DENY YOURSELF OR DENY YOUR LORD: The Daily Cross of Luke 9:23.”
paragraphs: “DENY YOURSELF OR DENY YOUR LORD: The Daily Cross of Luke 9:23.”

It sounds harsh until you’ve tried it, and then it sounds honest. “If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Me.” Daily. Not once at youth camp. Not after a dramatic crisis. Daily—as in this morning when you woke up with a hundred tiny urges, each volunteering to be king of your heart.

I used to think “deny yourself” meant becoming a smaller, sadder version of me—an edited person with all the color drained out. But that’s not the call. Denying yourself isn’t hating who you are; it’s dethroning who you are. It’s refusing to let your preferences run the kingdom while Christ is in the room. It’s trading the loud itch of impulse for the steady voice of the Shepherd. It’s inconvenient and, strangely, liberating—like unshouldering a backpack you didn’t realize you were carrying.

What makes this hard isn’t ignorance; it’s intimacy. You know your appetites. They know your schedule. They whisper in accents you trust: “You deserve this.” “You’re the exception.” “One more time won’t hurt.” Denial, in our ears, sounds like loss. Jesus reframes it as direction. He doesn’t say, “Deny yourself and stop there.” He says, “Deny yourself…and follow.” The point isn’t self-erasure; it’s re-alignment. You say no to a smaller love so you can say yes to a larger One.

Let’s ground this in Tuesdays, not theories. You’re scrolling late, eyes gritty, mind tired. A link glows like candy. Deny yourself means closing the tab for love of the One who calls your body a temple, not a vending machine. Or you’ve drafted the perfect clapback that will win the argument and lose your soul. Deny yourself looks like deleting the zinger, blessing the person, and going to bed unvictorious in public but clean in heart. Or money—always money. The toy you want and the tithe that pinches. Deny yourself sounds like a lousy financial strategy until you realize generosity is how you end the tyranny of “mine.”

Is this legalism? Not even close. Legalism is behavior for applause. The daily cross is obedience for love. Legalism hunts for loopholes so it can brag. The daily cross hunts for the first yes so Christ can reign. Grace isn’t opposed to effort; it’s opposed to earning. If the word “deny” makes you bristle, ask what part of you is being protected by that bristle. Often it’s the part that’s quietly exhausting you.

There’s a story I keep replaying. A guy named Ramon—workaholic, good heart, thin patience—told me he began practicing a “morning dying.” Nothing mystical. Before checking his phone, he’d sit on the edge of the bed and pray, “Jesus, I resign from being my own lord today. Here are my plans. Edit them.” Then he’d name three places he knew he’d be tempted to self-rule: his temper in traffic, his pride in meetings, his appetite after 9 p.m. He didn’t always nail it. But the naming mattered. It was like choosing where to plant the cross before the battle started. Over time, his wife said he became gentler. Not softer, gentler. Denial didn’t shrink him; it rooted him.

Maybe you’re wondering where joy fits in. If the Christian life is one long no, who survives it? Here’s the paradox that stubbornly refuses to go away: every time I deny a lesser love, my capacity for joy grows. When I say no to the fixation that numbs me, I can actually taste food again, music again, Scripture again. The Spirit’s fruit—love, joy, peace, patience—is not grown in a greenhouse of indulgence. It ripens in the open air of obedience. Joy isn’t the reward for never messing up; it’s the consequence of letting Jesus be Lord in places I used to protect.

Still, I won’t pretend every no feels noble in the moment. Sometimes it feels like dying because—let’s be blunt—it is. A death to the self that insists on center stage. A death to the storyline where I’m the hero and God is a side character with miracle cameos. We don’t get resurrection without death, but we’d love to negotiate a loophole: “Lord, could we do resurrection-ish?” He smiles. We pick up the cross. And somehow, while we’re carrying it, He’s carrying us.

If Luke 9:23 is the headline, what’s the fine print? Jesus says daily. The frequency matters because memory is short and drift is real. Daily doesn’t mean dramatic. It means ordinary faithfulness with a stubborn rhythm. Here are a few ways that rhythm can sound, unpolished but livable:

Start with a surrendered sentence. Before the algorithm catechizes you, give Christ the first word. “Jesus, You’re Lord; I’m not. Lead me.” Write it on a card. Tape it where you brush your teeth. The body remembers what the eyes repeat.

Pick one habit to crucify for a season. Not everything, one thing. Maybe it’s the doom scroll after midnight or the casual gossip that feels like community. Name it. Nail it. Replace it with a simple practice that opens room for the Spirit—a psalm aloud, a phone call of encouragement, a quiet walk where you pray the Lord’s Prayer line by line.

Practice pre-decisions. Decide at breakfast how you’ll answer the bossy appetites later. “When I’m tempted to lie, I’ll tell the truth and accept the consequence.” “When I want to buy the shiny thing, I’ll wait 48 hours and pray.” Pre-decisions turn emergency rooms into planned surgeries.

Put your money where your throne is. Generosity is a sledgehammer to the idol of self. Set aside first, not leftover. Give where the Gospel is preached and the poor are remembered. You’ll feel the pinch. That pinch is the sound of chains breaking.

Invite a cross-bearing friend. Lone-wolf holiness becomes weird fast. Meet weekly with one person who can ask, “Where did you deny yourself? Where did you deny your Lord?” Celebrate the yeses. Drag the no’s into the light without drama. Pray like people who are still learning how to walk.

Receive the ordinary crosses. Some crosses arrive without your vote: chronic pain, unfair criticism, the long patience of loving difficult people. Don’t romanticize them; don’t waste them either. Offer them back to Jesus: “I don’t like this, but I’ll carry it with You. Grow Christ in me through this weight.”

And when you fail—and you will—refuse the cheap exit of shame. Shame performs penitence while keeping self at the center. Repentance surrenders and moves. The cross you dropped yesterday can be lifted today. The grace that saved you is the grace that trains you. The Lord you denied with a quick temper is the Lord who cooks breakfast on the shore and says, “Do you love Me? Follow Me.”

The quiet scandal of Luke 9:23 is that Jesus invites us into the same pattern He lived. He denied Himself, took up His cross, and walked ahead of us through death into life. He doesn’t demand from a distance; He disciples up close. The daily cross is not an instrument of self-hatred; it’s the doorway to being truly human. Less fake peace, more real holiness. Less frantic wanting, more deep contentment. Less performing, more presence.

A friend once told me the daily cross felt like carrying a ladder: always awkward, always bumping into things. Now, years in, he says it feels more like carrying a key—still weighty, but it opens doors no shortcut ever could. He laughs more. He apologizes faster. He sleeps without that buzzing anxiety that used to hum behind his eyes. Denying himself didn’t make him lesser; it made him free enough to love without negotiating his own throne.

So tomorrow, before the world starts tugging at your sleeves, choose your cross. Not as a grim ritual, but as a yes to the One who is worth more than a thousand easy days. Deny the appetite that keeps you small. Deny the lie that you are your own. Deny the script where comfort equals blessing. And then, with shoulders squared and heart listening, follow—the next right step, the next honest prayer, the next unseen kindness. It won’t make headlines. It will make a disciple. And somewhere in that daily dying, you’ll notice something rising that you cannot manufacture: a quiet, durable joy that sounds a lot like freedom.
